SOURCE: "REALM: Retrieval-Augmented Language Model Pre-Training", Kelvin Guu*, Kenton Lee*, Zora Tung, Panupong Pasupat, Ming-Wei Chang (Google Research). The extraction is arXiv 2002.08909v1, dated 10 Feb 2020. That copy has no ICML header, so "ICML 2020" is not confirmed by the PDF itself.

COVERAGE: I read all 50,583 of 50,583 extracted characters across 12 pages, including the body, Tables 1–4, Appendices A–D (gradient derivation, link to supervised learning, adapting to new knowledge, retrieval utility) and Figure 4. I skimmed the references (pp. 9–10) for origins. Nothing was skipped.

CLAIMS
- claim: REALM beats every earlier Open-QA system on all three benchmarks while reading only 5 documents.
  number: NQ 39.2 / WQ 40.2 / CT 46.8 (X=Wikipedia); NQ 40.4 / WQ 40.7 / CT 42.9 (X=CC-News); both 330m params
  setup: test-set exact match. NQ has 79k/4k train/test, WQ 3k/2k, CT 1k/1k. The knowledge corpus Z is English Wikipedia, 20 Dec 2018 snapshot, split into chunks of up to 288 wordpieces, which gives just over 13M candidates. Fine-tuning retrieves the top 5. The encoder starts from BERT-base uncased.
  quote: "Ours (X = Wikipedia, Z = Wikipedia) Dense Retr. +Transformer REALM 39.2 40.2 46.8 330m" / "Ours (X = CC-News, Z = Wikipedia) Dense Retr. +Transformer REALM 40.4 40.7 42.9 330m"
  where: p7, Table 1
- claim: Abstract margin over previous methods.
  number: 4-16% absolute
  setup: same three benchmarks
  quote: "we outperform all previous methods by a significant margin (4-16% absolute accuracy)"
  where: p1, abstract
- claim: A 330m-parameter REALM beats T5-11B, which stores knowledge only in its parameters and is about 30x larger. Growing T5 50x adds only about 5 points.
  number: T5-11B NQ 34.5 / WQ 37.4 at 11318m params; T5-base 27.0 / 29.1 at 223m
  setup: Table 1. T5 was not evaluated on CuratedTrec because its answers are regexes. T5 also saw SQuAD during pre-training.
  quote: "from Base to 11B, the model is 50 times larger, and gains roughly 5 points in accuracy). In contrast, REALM outperforms the largest T5-11B model while being 30 times smaller."
  where: p7, Sec 4.4
- claim: Compared with ORQA, the fine-tuning setup is identical, so the whole gain comes from REALM pre-training.
  number: ORQA NQ 33.3 / WQ 36.4 / CT 30.1, also 330m
  quote: "The improvement of REALM over ORQA is purely due to better pre-training methods."
  where: p7, Table 1 and Sec 4.4
- claim: A 30x staler index during pre-training collapses performance to below the ORQA baseline. Index freshness matters for joint training.
  number: NQ dev EM 38.2 → 28.7; zero-shot Recall@5 38.5 → 15.1. Baseline ORQA is 31.3 / 13.9.
  setup: NQ dev set. The normal setup refreshes about once every 500 steps. The paper does not state the 30x interval as a step count, but it implies about 15k steps.
  quote: "30× stale MIPS 28.7 15.1" and "This results in one index refresh per approximately 500 training steps."
  where: p7 Table 2; p8 Sec 4.5
- claim: The index goes stale after every retriever update. REALM rebuilds it asynchronously every few hundred steps and re-scores the top k with fresh parameters.
  number: "every several hundred training steps"
  quote: "the search index goes “stale” after every gradient update on θ. Our solution is to “refresh” the index by asynchronously re-embedding and re-indexing all documents every several hundred training steps."
  where: p4, Sec 3.3
- claim: Refresh runs as two parallel jobs, a trainer and an index builder. The document-embedding step uses 16 TPUs.
  number: 16 TPUs (index); 64 TPUs (trainer)
  setup: 200k steps, batch 512, lr 3e-5, 8 candidate documents per example including the null document
  quote: "We pre-train for 200k steps on 64 Google Cloud TPUs, with a batch size of 512 and a learning rate of 3e-5 ... The document embedding step for the MIPS index is parallelized over 16 TPUs. For each example, we retrieve and marginalize over 8 candidate documents, including the null document ∅."
  where: p7, Sec 4.3
- claim: Fine-tuning never refreshes the document index. Only the query encoder is updated, and the whole model fits on one 12GB GPU.
  number: 12GB
  quote: "For fine-tuning, we just build the MIPS index once (using the pre-trained θ) for simplicity and do not update Embeddoc. Note that we still fine-tune Embedinput" ; "entire model can be run on a single machine with a 12GB GPU."
  where: p5 Sec 3.3; p7
- claim: Salient span masking, which masks named entities and dates, is crucial. Random token masks and SpanBERT-style random span masks do clearly worse.
  number: EM / Recall@5 = 38.2/38.5 (salient) vs 32.3/24.2 (random uniform) vs 35.3/26.1 (random span)
  setup: NQ dev. Entities come from a BERT tagger trained on CoNLL-2003; dates come from a regex.
  quote: "REALM with random uniform masks 32.3 24.2" / "REALM with random span masks 35.3 26.1"; "it is crucial for REALM"
  where: p7 Table 2; p5 Sec 3.4; p8
- claim: Both components gain from joint pre-training, and the best result needs both. The retriever carries most of the gain.
  number: REALM retriever + baseline encoder 37.4; baseline retriever + REALM encoder 35.3; full 38.2; ORQA 31.3
  quote: "REALM retriever+Baseline encoder 37.4 38.5" / "Baseline retriever+REALM encoder 35.3 13.9"; "the best result requires both components acting in unison."
  where: p7 Table 2; p8
- claim: The retriever gradient rewards a document exactly when it predicts y better than the average retrieved document.
  number: none
  quote: "document z receives a positive update whenever it performs better than expected."
  where: p5, Sec 3.3; full derivation in App A, p11
- claim: The marginal over the corpus is approximated by the top-k documents from MIPS.
  number: none
  quote: "We approximate this by instead summing over the top k documents with highest probability under p(z | x)—this is reasonable if most documents have near zero probability."
  where: p4
- claim: Other retrieval-based systems read 20–80 documents, while REALM reads 5.
  number: 20 to 80 vs 5
  quote: "which often retrieve from 20 to 80 documents, our system gets the overall best performance while only retrieving 5 documents."
  where: p7
- claim: Without the cold-start fixes training collapses. The retriever is warm-started with ICT, a null document acts as a sink, and trivial self-retrieval is excluded.
  number: none
  quote: "This causes the knowledge augmented encoder to learn to ignore the retrieved documents. Once this occurs, the knowledge retriever does not receive a meaningful gradient and cannot improve, creating a vicious cycle."
  where: p5, Sec 3.4
- claim: Swapping in a newer corpus can update answers without retraining, but only partly.
  number: none; this is a single qualitative example (Table 4, 2018 vs 2020 Wikipedia)
  quote: "the knowledge-augmented encoder will still end up remembering some world knowledge, making the prediction of some input sentences not updated with the new corpus."
  where: p11, App C

LIMITS
- No refresh-interval sweep. The paper tests only about 500 steps against "30x stale", with one run on the NQ dev set and no variance reported. It does not measure the cost of a refresh, such as wall-clock time, TPU-hours or rebuild time. 16 TPUs for embedding is the only cost figure.
- Fine-tuning freezes the document index, which is itself a concession to cost. Footnote 3: "it is possible that refreshing the index would further improve performance."
- It is extractive QA only. Answers must be spans, and there is no generative reader.
- T5 had SQuAD data and REALM did not. CuratedTrec has no generative baselines.
- Ablations cover NQ dev only. The corpus-update evidence is anecdotal (App C).
- It is dated. The models are BERT-base scale with 288-wordpiece chunks, and the authors call this a "minimal instantiation" (p9). Later end-to-end retrieve-and-generate work superseded the extractive setup.

BUILDS ON
- ORQA (Lee et al., 2019): same latent-variable formulation, ICT warm start, and identical fine-tuning hyperparameters.
- BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) for the encoders and the MLM objective. SpanBERT (Joshi et al., 2019) is the masking comparator.
- MIPS: Ram & Gray, 2012; Shrivastava & Li, 2014; Shen et al., 2015.
- Retrieve-then-read Open-QA: Chen et al., 2017 (DrQA); Brill et al., 2002.
- kNN-LM (Khandelwal et al., 2019) for contrast.
- Retrieve-and-edit: Guu et al., 2018; Hashimoto et al., 2018.
- Memory networks / product-key memory: Weston et al., 2014; Lample et al., 2019.
- T5 closed-book baseline: Roberts et al., 2020.

CODE: none. The paper has no code listings. The core equation, verbatim from the extraction on p3, is "p(y | x) = ∑ z∈Z p(y | z, x) p(z | x). (1)".

FIGURES
- Figure 3, p5: "REALM pre-training with asynchronous MIPS refreshes." This is the best candidate for "The two components" and the stale-index section. It shows the trainer sending a parameter snapshot θ′ to the index builder, which returns a new index while training continues. That loop is faster to grasp as a picture than in prose.
- Figure 2, p4 (alternative): "The overall framework of REALM. Left: Unsupervised pre-training ... Right: Supervised fine-tuning." It shows retriever θ and encoder φ trained jointly, then fine-tuned.
- Figure 4, p12: retrieval utility over pre-training steps for the three masking schemes. Use it if the note covers salient span masking.

PROBLEMS
- pypdf printed fontTools warnings on stderr. The text itself is clean, apart from small spacing faults such as "Approache s" and "langua ge", and ligatures (fi→ﬁ) that may need normalising in quotes.
- The math in equations is flattened, but it is still readable.
- The PDF contains no embedded instructions.
- The ICML venue is not visible in this arXiv v1 copy.
